notes.meaning: David wrote this after the prophet Nathan faced him about his adultery with Bathsheba and the death of her husband Uriah. He does not point to his good deeds. He leans only on God's steady love and deep kindness. He asks God to 'blot out' his rebellions, like wiping a debt or a charge off a record.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have doubted that the heading fits the psalm. They point to verse 4 ('against You only') and verses 18-19. Others answer that the whole psalm still sounds like David.

notes.meaning: David feels his sin is like a deep stain soaked into cloth. He asks God to wash him again and again until it is fully gone. Nathan had already told him he was forgiven. Still, David keeps asking, so that the pardon might become clearer and surer to him.

David openly owns what he did and makes no excuses. His sin is always on his mind, and it fills him with sorrow and shame. Real repentance (turning away from sin with sorrow) is not a passing feeling. It is a lasting grief over having done wrong.

David knows he hurt Bathsheba, Uriah and many others. But the deepest wrong was against God, whose law he broke while God watched. He agrees that God is fair in whatever judgment He gives. Paul later quotes this verse in Romans 3:4.

David traces his sin back to its root, a sinful nature he has had from the very start of life. Christians call this 'original sin': the bent toward evil every person is born with. He is not blaming his mother or making an excuse. He is making his confession complete.

God wants more than right actions. He wants honesty and truth deep in the heart. This shows David how far he had fallen, since he had lied and schemed. Yet it also gives him hope that God will teach him wisdom on the inside.

Hyssop was a small plant used to sprinkle water or blood when cleansing lepers and others who were 'unclean' under the law. David asks God Himself to cleanse him this way. Christian writers see here the blood of Christ washing away sin. 'Whiter than snow' means made fully clean, as in Isaiah 1:18.

Guilt has hurt David so much that he feels like his bones have been crushed. He asks for joy only after asking to be cleansed. He wants to hear God's comforting word of pardon, so that his crushed spirit can rejoice again.
David's sin is always before his own eyes. So he asks God to look away from it and not deal with him as he deserves. He repeats his first prayer but adds 'all': blot out every one of my sins.

Forgiveness is not enough for David. He wants a changed heart. The word 'create' is used only of God's work, because only God can make a heart new. A 'right spirit' means a steady, faithful spirit that will not wander again.

David begs not to be shut out from God's presence and favor. He knows he has grieved the Holy Spirit. He remembers how the Spirit left King Saul. More than his crown or his life, he dreads losing God's Spirit.

differ.view: David's sin was serious enough that the Spirit could rightly leave him for good, and then all hope would be gone. But any godly sorrow and longing for mercy shows the Spirit has not yet left.

notes.meaning: David once knew the joy of being saved, and he lost it through sin. He asks God to give it back. He also asks God to hold him up with a willing, free spirit. That means one freed from slavery to sin, so he can gladly do what is right.

Once he is forgiven, David promises to teach other sinners God's ways. He will show them how to turn back and how ready God is to forgive. Through this very psalm, he is still teaching people to repent.

Now David names his sin plainly as 'bloodguilt', the guilt of causing Uriah's death. Yet he calls on God more boldly as 'the God of my salvation.' Once he is freed, he will sing loudly of God's righteousness, His goodness in forgiving.
Guilt and shame had shut David's mouth, so he could not praise God. He asks the Lord to open his lips by taking away that guilt. Then his mouth will be free to praise God for His forgiving mercy.

David would gladly offer any number of animals if that could take away his sin. But animal sacrifices could not truly pay for sin. The law gave no sacrifice to cover deliberate murder and adultery. A 'burnt offering' was an animal burned whole on the altar.

What God truly wants is a broken spirit and a 'contrite' heart, one crushed with humble sorrow for sin. People look down on what is broken, but God will never turn away such a heart. Only Christ's sacrifice pays for sin. A broken heart is our offering of honest sorrow to God.

David knew his sin could bring trouble on the whole nation. So he prays that God would still bless Zion and build up Jerusalem's walls. Once God and His people are at peace again, their offerings, given with a right heart, will please Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think these two verses were added later, during the exile, when Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins. Others reply that the walls were still being built in David's day, so the prayer fits him.
